title: Claude Code's "Don't Ask Again" exposes passwords in 1,122 public GitHub files (apiiro.com)
comments: Boris from the Claude Code team here. Historically Claude Code has not done secret scrubbing (there are many good tools for that), but we are looking into what we can do to prevent this.That said, a few thoughts:1. .claude/settings.local.json is meant to stay local. This is not a file you should check into source control. We automatically gitignore it when Claude creates the file, so in this case the files were manually created and checked in (docs: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings)2. Permission rules are old hat. Everyone should be using auto mode instead. It is safer and also does not require manually maintaining finicky allow/deny lists. Auto mode is enabled by default and is included for free in all plans.3. Regardless of what agent you use, you should have secret scanning enabled. GitHub and other source control hosts offer it. There are many threat models that it protects against and you should absolutely use it if you can. (see https://github.com/security/plans)reply

Auto mode cannot be considered safer than anything because it does not even attempt to guarantee any sort of security. The threat model is not even defined. It cannot be quantified or compared with any other approach other than "full access"reply

Compare approving every step manually: at first you read everything the llm proposes carefully, convinced that you'll catch it out. After a while you get faster and faster until at some point you find yourself hitting "approve" the second the text appears, long before you actually could absorb what it said.This is called "approval fatigue".If you think this can't possibly happen to you, you might be in for a surprise.  This is an almost textbook case of classic conditioning. You'll find yourself hitting that button faster and faster even while fighting back the urge. So a human is no guaranteed backstop.This is the scenario that cc auto mode guards against. It cuts down the number of permission prompts to something manageable, so that your fingers don't get trained into clicking 'approve' on 'rm -rf' in the very eyeblink that it appears.So maybe you feel it doesn't work in theory; but weirdly enough, in practice this particular approach is actually one of the better ones; especially when used in combination with other common sense measures where practical.reply

I'm not claiming auto is worse than manual; I'm claiming it cannot be compared with anything security-wise because it does not aim to provide any guarantees, there's no systematic way to reason about what it will and won't allow, etcWith e.g. VM or container sandboxing, we can say things like "If there are no vulnerabilities in the hypervisor or hardware, then the agent can only access these files, these network services, etc". Auto mode doesn't even try to provide any guarantees, so it's impossible to reason about. It amounts to just using the models judgment about what's "malicious" or not, a definition which is subjective, changes model to model, and can be influenced by attacker input.Empirical evaluations of how many vulnerabilities manual vs auto mode let through are not super meaningful because auto mode changes dramatically with model releases, the type of task being performed, whether the attacker is making targeted attacks designed to bypass auto mode, etc. A security feature cannot rely on these sorts of factors if it's to be taken seriously.Further, percent of malicious tool calls accepted is a bad metric. It's like measuring the security of ssh in terms of what percent of unauthenticated logins succeed. The only acceptable value is zero. It's pass/fail, not a spectrum. So both auto and manual mode should fail equally here. Further, the set of malicious tool calls admitted in auto mode may not be a subset of those admitted in manual mode.reply

Ah, you're going for the actual adversarial case.I think I'd trust the current approver with correctly classifying regular semi-interactive LLM behavior fairly well.However, if we bring in a hostile adversary that calculus changes, and you'd be right to start thinking about other approaches.On the other hand, transformers are a surprisingly powerful technology, and I wonder if there wouldn't be ways to train one to several nines reliability  under adversarial attack. It seems to have worked in at least one case; though I'd be a bit cautious to extend that conclusion to more cases quite yet.* https://hackmyclaw.com/ ; https://simonwillison.net/2026/Jun/26/hack-my-ai-assistant/reply
Hmm, what does auto mode protect against in the non-adversarial case? Aren't the models already extensively trained not to perform harmful actions without provocation?reply

It mostly stops honest mistakes, because those do happen, especially when the <prompting> might not have been perfect either.You do have a bit of a point, though: I’ve run several models in sandboxes with --dangerously-skip-permissions for months; in the full expectation that I'd need to replace a sandbox once in a while. But so far none of the sandboxes have trashed themselves, yet. knock on woodAuto mode seems like a lighter-weight version of that: fewer local resources, and it can run on the metal if you need cc to help with system work.reply

Auto mode is significantly safer than manual approval in practice. Details about the engineering approach and how we tested whether it is safer here: https://claude.com/resources/articles/auto-mode-default-in-c....reply

Auto mode may be significantly safer in the niche case where you want the model to have free reign, in a fully unopinionated environment, where it's allowed to make any changes and make any external calls.Many of the problems when it comes to the manual approval feel like they stem from the expectation of using auto mode in the first place. After all, what's the point of improving the manual approval and safety matching if auto mode is the end all be all, and what's the point of training the model to output commands in a manner that can be parsed by a human if auto mode is always meant to be used? It's very rare for me to not see "command could not be statically analyzed", because the model keeps outputting bash golf.reply

> in the niche case where you want the model to have free reign, in a fully unopinionated environment, where it's allowed to make any changes and make any external calls.That is not the niche case, that's the dominant use of models.It would be helpful to distinguish between your own opinion on how models ought to be used, compared to how others actually use models.reply

title: Making any integer with four 2s (2025) (thegreenplace.net)
comments: i know everyone plays with their own rules, but from my perspective, a square root spends a 2 - it's not an operator like + or ! . there's an implicit "2" since you could also take the cube root or fourth rootreply
You can use `sin(arctan())` as the repeatable operator instead of sqrt(). Then "unwrap" by applying ^-2 - (2^-2)3=(sin(arctan(sin(arctan(sin(arctan(2))))))^−2 − (2)^−2reply
> it's not an operator like + or !Squaring is to multiplication as is the latter to addition. If roots are invalid then so should be multiplications.reply
Exponentiation is to multiplication as multiplication is to addition. Squaring is to multiplication as doubling is to addition.reply

GP didn't say roots are invalid, just that they burn a two.If we agree that 2^2 uses two twos (and, indeed, that 2^3 isn't valid, because it uses a 3), then what's the equivalent of a square root?Of course to my simple math brain, a square root is ^1/2, which includes the digit 1. But I agree there is someone 2-ish about the square root.reply
Would you elaborate on that? That doesn't make any sense to mereply

Multiplication is repeated addition.2x3= 2+2+2
AxB= A+A B times.Raising to a power is repeated multiplication.2^3= 2x2x2
A^B = AxA B timesRoots are the inverse of powersDivision is the inverse of multiplications.Given this… the OC’s comment  about giving exceptions to powers in the rules is nonsense because they are still operations.reply

Multiplication is not the same as repeated addition, which you can observe as soon as you try the two different operations on fractions or negative numbers. For example, you can't add a number to itself 1/3 times, but you can certainly scale a number by 1/3.Multiplication is a scaling operation.reply

Because it's just wrong. hahajk said that taking the 2nd root spends a 2, not that "roots are invalid". (FWIW, I'm not necessarily endorsing the view that the square root symbol implicitly spends a 2, I'm just saying that the counterarguments given are logically wrong ... actually more like semantically wrong.)The comment below by drfloyd51 is similarly wrong ... hahajk didn't say anything about "giving exceptions to powers in the rules".And the comment by speglt is also wrong:> If taking a square root is an inherent use of a two, then dividing a number by another number should also be a use of a two, because there are two operands.The number of operands isn't relevant; the degree of the root is.And from SideQuark we get> One could even claim division is raising to the -1 power, thereby disqualifying it in exactly the same manner you disqualify sqrt.But hahajk said nothing about anything being disqualified. (Not to mention that division is not raising to the -1 power ... raising what? n/d = n * d^-1, but this is completely irrelevant to hahajk's argument.)reply

Multiplication is adding numbers to themselves. Exponentiation is multiplying numbers by themselves. Ditto division/taking roots. Squaring a number is just the instance of exponentiation that happens to have two operands. If taking a square root is an inherent use of a two, then dividing a number by another number should also be a use of a two, because there are two operands.reply

comments:

 - Everything on one page, information dense
 - Focus on code and unresolved discussions, maybe CI checks
 - Keyboard navigationGraphite gets pretty close! But it's become cluttered over the years. CodeApprove is far from perfect too (it's been a while since I worked on the UX much) but I'd hope GitHub could do a little better.reply

We’ve been building our own Review Pipeline, including automated review guides, risk detection and much more.There’s SO much to be done around Code Review, I’m very surprised GitHub isn’t doing more.They have the reach already, they have years of real review data. And yet, the PR itself is not using any of the newly available methods for more efficient review.Agents are hammering PRs out left and right, and yet here I am still staring at the raw diff of 35 PRs and end up being called the bottleneck.reply
Code review process is the worst part of LLM-assisted SDLC at the moment, probably because nobody knows how to do it well yet.reply

I at least:Use CI results to control quality, no nitpicking style means easier reviewReview tests one by one, to make sure I understand what the submitter is trying to test and if they actually did soCheck files off one-by-one, compartmentalizing understanding as I goComplain loudly when PRs try to change too many subsystems or different functionality, especially if less related changes are not separated into standalone commitsreply
I mean if it's a code review, you gotta review the code.reply

Yes, but code can be presented in different ways. This depends of course to a degree on the submitter (large changeset touching a lot of files or smaller change sets building upon each other?) but also could be presented differently (highlighting changes to data structures, identifying core parts of code and helper routines - lots of room for imagination)Also mind: one doesn't only have to review changes code, but also review what hasn't been changed (are preconditions of other code still met?)reply

I've been trying to auto generate diagrams on PRs I'm reviewing. Flows changes via sequence diagrams, state changes and schema changes, post it to the PR with a skill. Then look at the relevant code based on the diagrams. Then \code-reviews. Moderately helpful. YMMVreply

I don’t believe that nobody is doing it well. May I ask who is doing it well? Either in house or with an AI reviewer vendor.For me, what works is highly templated directory structure and rules that linters can quickly check and enforce. Every PR is a cookie cutter design filled in. There are only a handful of things you need and they’re all just CRUD at the end of the day. You can employ the same very few design patterns and primitives across a lot of your stack. Review is so fast, if you trust your CI to do its job and the developer to actually QA their own work.What isn’t working is the sheer volume of PRs. Even with CODEOWNERS directing attention to only high impact changes, it is a constant distraction. I’m not sure how to handle SOC2 where we need a human reviewer on all code. Lastly, agents shit the bed when they touch spaghetti, esp when it’s sitting next to structured patterns. IME, the best way to get around this is to just rewrite features from scratch. But in this current world of instant completion and reward, it’s been challenging to convince people to commit to more ambitious lifts.Finally, I want review more than ever. A team can’t keep up with the pace of change even if it was all perfect. I like the idea of more up front planning, but the code is ultimately what matters.reply

I’m waiting to see someone who has any sort of reasonable way, but I have yet to see one. Code review was always a difficult part of the job. However, it was self regulating because the people who would do very large code dumps frequently were very very few high throughput individuals and they were either legitimately good and knew what they were doing, so you trusted them, or were quickly told to not do that. The process had natural breaks on it, and particularly large PR would be expected to take few days or week(s) to review.This all has changed. I’ve only seen gaslighting (in the form of “of course we expect you to read the code LLMs is generating”), lying along the same lines, or the realistic people who acknowledge they don’t read any of it. The former camp is mostly traditional engineers, and the later is mostly new or traditional non-engineering roles like recent product management coding converts. I think it would help everyone if we just normalize the fact that no one if reading code much anymore. It’s just not feasible. Write a bunch of creative reviewing bots or SKILLs and just leave it at that. It’s not a great answer, but like I said I haven’t seen any alternatives.> if you trust your CI to do its job and the developer to actually QA their own work.I trust the CI, but the CI is doing what the CI is written to do. I don’t know how you can achieve the second part in a large team/corporate setting or an open source setting.reply
first_paragraph: On a long pull request, checking what’s blocking often means scrolling past dozens of comments and timeline events just to reach the merge box. And once you’re there, you still need to work out what to do next. As people need to review more and more pull requests, time spent scrolling adds up. So we’ve begun to rethink the entire experience, beginning with addressing a familiar challenge: finding what’s blocking progress and determining what to do next.Today, we’re introducing the Overview page as an opt-in public preview, with rollout continuing through the weekend. It brings merge status and next available actions to the top of the page in a compact readiness summary. It’s the first step toward making pull requests easier to follow as code, conversations, and reviews evolve.We’re starting with the merge box, the place developers go to see whether a pull request can move forward. Rather than just moving it higher, we’ve also redesigned it to show the same information in less than half

title: MaxxBench – "Nice DeepSWE score. But is it true?" (unlap.ai)
comments: This is a great example of how to test how well a benchmark score generalises. The first order approximation is not complicated: just vary a parameter and see how much the score changes.Which parameter to vary depends on the result of the test, but the MaxxBench route of varying the task spec seems like a good default, though not always the most informative.In one of my private benchmarks I realised many of the less capable models didn't fail because they submitted the wrong answer, but because they exceeded their budget for number of tool calls they were allowed. The more capable models never got close to the tool call limit because they tended toward combining tool calls (e.g. chaining multiple shell commands in one Bash tool call).Was my benchmark actually measuring ability to combine tool calls rather than reasoning ability on the problem at hand? Well, easy enough to find out: re-run under a different tool call budget and see how much the scores change.(Next problem: is ability to combine tool calls a useful thing to measure, i.e. should it confer an advantage in the benchmark? It could be if it is a sign of planning multiple steps ahead.)reply

Historically, that happens now and then. Examples include color television cameras and fluorescent lamp ballasts.RCA developed the first good color TV cameras. They were monsters. Originally, electronic TV (as opposed to mechanical scanning) used Zworykin's iconoscope. This needed huge amounts of light. It didn't have a photo-multiplier stage                              to boost sensitivity, but it did accumulate charge from light over the whole frame time. There was an alternative approach, Farnsworth's image dissector, which also needed huge amounts of light. It had a photo-multiplier stage but only the light from the dot currently being scanned by the scanning beam mattered.So RCA threw money at the problem. They developed the image orthicon camera tube. It combined the advantages of both approaches, integration over a full frame and a photo-multiplier stage. It was insanely expensive, costing thousands of dollars in the 1950s. It needed about twenty different voltages and multiple independent power supplies. It worked reasonably well.Then came color. That took three image orthicons (RGB) inside a box the size of a small refrigerator, along with optics to split the incoming image into three colors. Plus 
a rack of analog electronics per camera, connected through a large cable. Plus an alignment problem from hell, with a huge number of adjustment knobs.[1]Scaling worked! From the 1950s to the 1970s, color TV broadcasting was powered by those monsters.Now, independent of this, other people were working on other approaches. Vidicons, silicon detectors inside camera tubes, and finally fully solid state image sensors. Eventually, in 
1983, after thirty years of image orthicon monsters, RCA produced a usable solid state camera. Today, a cell phone camera costs about US$10 in bulk, and it's far better than the monsters.It took thirty years of low-priority development to get past the giant image orthicon cameras.Electronic fluorescent lamp ballasts had a different problem. That was a suppressed invention.
The magnetic ballast industry was dominated by Magnetek. Someone invented a solid state replacement, which was smaller and cheaper, and licensed their patent to Magnetek for royalties. Magnetek just sat on it, not wanting to gut their core market. The inventor hired Townsend, Townsend and Crew in Palo Alto and sued. (Read this in the law firm's brag book in their office.) Eventually, the inventor got a hundred million or so, solid state ballasts went into production, and Magnetek seems to be gone. (The company called Magnetek today, which makes crane controls, is an offshoot of a Litton unit, and seems to be unrelated.)There are also parallels from the steam locomotive industry, the Baldwin Locomotive Works being the best known. Baldwin actually built the first Diesel locomotive. They made a few half-hearted tries at Diesels over several decades, then gave up and went back to steam. Baldwin ceased all locomotive production in 1956. The corporation lingered on for a while, not doing much.[1] https://www.tvcameramuseum.org/rca/tk40a/pix/rcatk40aart.pdfreply

title: Commodore PET – The Worlds First Personal Computer (commodore.ca)
comments: Old man story time. This was the first computer we had in our home, I believe in the summer of 1978 or 1979.  Mom was working on her Masters in education (high school mathematics) and also taking Fortran courses on Hofstra’s PDP-11. She took me (~6 years old) to the machine room once, and one of the bearded sysadmins printed me a giant ASCII art of Snoopy on his doghouse on white and green fanfold paper with a dot matrix printer.Her high school took delivery of its first ever computer, a PET with a chiclet keyboard. She was assigned to take it home over the summer to learn, and figure out how to use in the curriculum.A few memories- it was the first piece of electronic equipment in the house with a grounded plug, and the house had no grounded outlets. Most people would have used a cheezy adapter, but Dad sledgehammered an 8’ copper rod in the backyard and installed a single grounded outlet for it.The cassette loading could be very fiddly and slow. A favorite game was “Hangman”, played that for hours. Observe the beautiful graphics.https://youtu.be/jnj2ZgOYYDQ?is=zZauKOy5f95wDqrgThe PET went back to the school in the fall, and I started begging for a PC of my own. For the longest time I was constantly asking for a Timex/Sinclair. Christmas 1983, a TI-99/4a appeared under the tree, thanks to them being sold far below cost after failing in the market. That lead to an Apple //e in 1987, and a Dell 486 DX2-66 in 1993.reply

>It was even one of the chief complaints about VS Code when it was first launched.That was absolutely not the case at all. At least not on HN or twitter. It was for Chief Complaints for Atom. When VS Code first launched everyone was suggesting how much faster it was compared to Atom. And how a properly tuned Electron Apps could be fast. And Microsoft promised it will get even faster that makes everyone excited.The only few of us who were complaining was how could everyone judge this to be fast when we have Sublime. And that was even before Sublime had GPU rendering.reply

I compared NP++ to VS Code at the time. VS Code was nice to use, but it was slower. It was faster than Visual Studio, but that's because VS Code without extensions didn't have language support, etc like VS did.I find it odd you see otherwise.And VS 2026 is faster than VS Code these days, now that they spent time optimizing it.reply
Googling if it was a common complaint around launch time shows plenty of threads on it across all the usual sites at that time.reply

I think OP is both right, and there was people still complaining about it. Atom was seriously slow. Everyone said you couldn’t build a fast text editor that could compare to native ones. VS Code came and it was significantly faster.  Atom was slow to the point of not being usable to some, while VS Code was perfectly usable. The people wanting vim or Sublime performance were still upset and wrote about it, but vscode was perfectly usable and fast enough for the majority of people. It was indeed held as an example of how to make a performant electron app. Still an electron app, but not absolute slog. Tbh, if you disable all extensions in vscode, it’s still fairly fast, and doesn’t even take that much memory. It’s not as usable without extensions though.reply

A huge pain of desktop development is managing dependencies particularly if you are coming from C++/Native code. Imagine you wanted to make a simple app in the 2010s that accesses the webcam for instance: If you use chrome you got the full html5 runtime, whereas with other tools you'd need bespoke libraries which your end user may not have.The only way to ship the same code between linux, macOS, and Windows would have been to either use something like Qt or the JVM back in the 2010s. The JVM desktop stuff was super ugly and Java itself had become notorious (also if you wanted anything remotely interesting like webcam/microphone or multimedia access you'd still have to ship dynamic libraries). Qt required special packaging skills to ship to the end user especially if third party libraries were involved. Electron killed that by bundling chrome (and chrome has a huge api surface).Today, I would argue the package management situation for a language like rust is a lot different. You dont have to cobble different DLLs together, you can just statically compile dependencies and cargo/rust do a pretty good job of making sure it's bundled with your app. Other languages also now have similarly useful tools.reply

But then the C++ libraries you mentioned also had the ability to statically link into a binary, which means you could statically link the webcam access in, in your example. So I don't see the advantage you're arguing for?reply

It comes down to package distribution.Chrome had already solved the hard problem of "how do we support webcams on linux, windows, and mac" and you as the dev just needed to use the Javascript webcam api. ( https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/MediaDevice... )In C++ land, you are ultimately going to either need to cook up your own webcam library or look for a 3rd party (which, in 2010, likely didn't exist) to provide it.Today, there are a few easy to discover rust crates which provide cross platform webcam apis.  But further, rust does cross platform better than C/C++ IMO.  It's really easy to change how code is compiled based on the target.  That was all well thought out because rust was supposed to be a language for browsers.reply

A cross platform webcam library isn't that hard to build at C++. I mean, it's tedious, and having to support multiple different operating systems makes it harder, so it certainly is going to cost a small pile of money, but this is not hard. The pile of money needed won't be all that large. Mind you, I prefer to use something that's off the shelf rather than writing my own, but it would not be hard to write my own.The hard part of all webcam libraries is all the different webcams running all their different proprietary protocols.reply
Qt is easily obtainable via vcpkg or conan.reply

first_paragraph:
As a one man game studio (an INDIEvidual) Bram Stolk develops games. This is his development diary.
  Yes, you read that right... for $8 you can run linux on a RISC-V computer.
  And not just a stripped down kernel without an MMU.
  No, the Ox64 comes with capable RISC-V cores.
  Heck, and not just one core, but three cores (all different.)
  Exciting times!

Caveat Emptor! At the time of writing, ethernet, wifi and SD-Card are not working. It's good to realize this before jumping into this.

  It looks like a microcontroller, but behaves like a UNIX machine. Sweet, or what? 
  Getting it up and running, though, is far from trivial.
  There are so many hurdles to take!

Hurdle 1: You cannot program it using USB, like you would an Arduino, ESP32, Stamp-C3 or rPi Pico.
  Nope... this needs to be programmed via the UART TX/RX pins.
  In the picture above, you can see them hooked up to GPIO14 / GPIO15 and GND.
